title: MYP Language Acquisition eAssessment Explained
summary: MYP Language Acquisition eAssessment explained for Year 5 students and parents, covering the on-screen exam, speaking assessment, criteria and grades.
body_markdown:
A Year 5 student opens a laptop and sees a text, an audio control and a countdown clock. Later, they sit across from their teacher for a structured conversation in a language that once felt unfamiliar.


Together, these moments form the **MYP Language Acquisition eAssessment** . Under current IB guidance, it is not a single examination and it is not an ePortfolio. It combines an externally marked on-screen examination with an individual speaking assessment conducted and marked by the school, then moderated by the IB.


The assessment measures four connected skills: listening, reading, speaking and writing. Each corresponds to one assessment criterion, and the combined result is converted into an MYP grade from 1 to 7.


For students, the practical lesson is simple. Success comes from communicating meaning across all four skills, not from memorising the largest possible vocabulary list.


### MYP Language Acquisition eAssessment at a glance


Feature Current format


Assessment route On-screen examination plus individual speaking assessment


On-screen duration Normally 1 hour 45 minutes


Skills tested on screen Listening, reading and writing


Speaking component Individual assessment organised and marked by the school, with IB moderation


Criteria A: Listening, B: Reading, C: Speaking, D: Writing


Proficiency The school registers the student at the appropriate level available for the language and session


Final result Grade 1 to 7


ePortfolio Not the assessment format for Language Acquisition


Students and parents who want the wider context can first review[what the IB Middle Years Programme involves](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-ib-middle-years-programme-explained-for-parents-and-students) and explore the[RevisionDojo MYP subject pages](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp) .


### Is it an on-screen exam or an ePortfolio?


This is the most common source of confusion about the MYP eAssessment format.


Some MYP subjects, including Arts, Design, and Physical and Health Education, use externally moderated ePortfolios. Language Acquisition takes a different route. According to the IB's current public guidance, its formal eAssessment consists of:


- one on-screen examination
- one internally assessed individual speaking assessment


The on-screen component normally lasts 1 hour 45 minutes. It assesses listening, reading and writing through interactive tasks based on spoken, written and visual material. The exact texts and prompts are unseen, but the language should connect to the prescribed course contexts and proficiency level.


The speaking component is completed separately. The school organises it, the teacher assesses it, and the IB moderates the results. Students should therefore ask their coordinator for the local date, preparation arrangements and language-specific instructions.


For a broader explanation of digital assessment, read[how MYP eAssessment works](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-does-myp-eassessment-work) and the guide to[MYP eAssessment examination lengths](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-long-are-myp-eassessment-exams) .


### Following a Year 5 student through the assessment


Imagine a capable Year 5 learner called Sam. Sam is studying an additional language and can communicate clearly, although unfamiliar accents and unexpected vocabulary still require concentration.


### First comes listening


Sam listens to spoken material and responds to questions that test more than isolated word recognition. A task may require the identification of a main idea, supporting detail, purpose, attitude or implied meaning.


Strong listeners use context before chasing every unknown word. They notice who is speaking, why the person is speaking and which details change the meaning. During revision, Sam can use **Study Notes** to review common text purposes, then use **Flashcards** for high-frequency vocabulary and connectors.


### Then comes reading


The reading section presents written and visual texts. Sam may need to retrieve information, interpret an opinion, connect evidence or explain how a message is communicated.


This is where careful evidence matters. An answer can sound plausible and still lose marks if it is not supported by the text. RevisionDojo's **Questionbank** can help students practise selecting evidence under time pressure rather than merely rereading vocabulary lists.


### Writing asks Sam to create meaning


Writing is not simply a grammar check. Sam must respond to a purpose, audience and context using an appropriate format and register. A message to a friend should not sound like a formal public statement, and a persuasive response needs more than a list of facts.


Before writing, Sam should identify four things: the required format, intended reader, purpose and essential content. RevisionDojo's **AI Chat** can help unpack prompts, while **Grading tools** can provide structured feedback on practice responses. Students should still compare that feedback with their teacher's interpretation of the official criterion.


### Speaking completes the picture


In the individual speaking assessment, Sam needs to sustain understandable communication rather than deliver a memorised script at high speed. Relevant ideas, interaction, pronunciation, vocabulary and grammatical control all contribute to an effective response.


A useful practice method is to record a response, listen once for meaning and listen again for language control. A **Tutor** can also challenge Sam with follow-up questions, which makes practice less predictable and closer to genuine interaction.


A student practises a family description at a laptop while a tie-wearing cat insists on being mentioned first.


*The household's strictest language examiner has entered the conversation.*


### The four MYP Language Acquisition criteria


The assessment is organised around four criteria. In ordinary school assessment, each criterion is commonly reported on a 0-8 achievement scale. The formal eAssessment uses task marks aligned with the same underlying skills.


Criterion Skill What the student must demonstrate


A Listening Understanding and interpreting spoken and multimodal communication


B Reading Understanding and interpreting written and visual communication


C Speaking Communicating ideas appropriately and effectively in speech


D Writing Communicating ideas appropriately and effectively in writing


The on-screen MYP Language Acquisition exam assesses Criteria A, B and D. Current assessment documentation allocates up to 32 raw marks to each of those areas, producing 96 on-screen marks. The individual speaking assessment covers Criterion C and carries up to 32 raw marks. This gives a combined total of 128 raw marks, with the on-screen component representing 75% and speaking representing 25% of the result.


That balance reveals something useful. A student cannot fully compensate for neglected speaking through written accuracy, or ignore listening because writing feels safer. The assessment rewards a balanced language user.


### How the final grade from 1 to 7 is reached


Classroom MYP grading and formal eAssessment grading are related, but they should not be treated as identical calculations.


For classroom reporting, teachers assess all four criteria, usually assigning an achievement level from 0 to 8 for each. Those levels produce a total out of 32, which the school converts using the relevant MYP boundaries. The[RevisionDojo guide to MYP criteria and grading](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-are-ib-myp-students-graded-criteria-explained) explains this model in more detail.


For the formal eAssessment, marks from the on-screen tasks and moderated speaking assessment are combined. The IB then applies subject and session grade boundaries to award a grade from 1 to 7.


There is no reliable universal raw-mark target that guarantees a 7 every year. Boundaries can reflect the assessment session and registered level, so students should not build a revision plan around an unofficial fixed percentage. A grade 7 represents consistently sophisticated, accurate and effective communication at the relevant proficiency level. Lower grades indicate progressively less secure understanding, control and transfer of language.


### A practical preparation plan


Good preparation resembles repeated conversation more than last-minute storage. Students need to retrieve language, interpret unfamiliar material and adapt it to a new purpose.


A balanced weekly cycle can look like this:


- complete one timed listening task and review why each error occurred
- annotate one reading text for purpose, audience, tone and evidence
- produce one planned writing response, then revise it against Criterion D
- record two short speaking responses and answer spontaneous follow-up questions
- review recurring vocabulary and grammar gaps with Flashcards


Use[MYP Language Acquisition examination strategies](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/language-acquisition-in-ib-myp-winning-strategies) to make that cycle more deliberate. **Predicted Papers** and **Mock Exams** can support timing and screen familiarity, while the **Questionbank** is better for focused skill practice. The **Coursework Library** is useful for understanding how criteria shape successful work, although the live examination still requires an independent response to unseen material.


Parents can help without becoming language teachers. Ask the student to explain the purpose of a task, protect regular practice time and encourage them to review feedback by criterion. The wider overview of[the eight MYP subject groups](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-subjects-are-taught-in-myp) can also help families understand where Language Acquisition fits within Year 5.


### The assessment is testing adaptability


The deepest challenge in the MYP Language Acquisition eAssessment is not knowing what will appear. It is using familiar language when the context changes.


That is why RevisionDojo works best as a connected system. Study Notes establish understanding. Flashcards strengthen retrieval. The Questionbank turns knowledge into decisions. AI Chat and Grading tools make feedback more immediate, while Mock Exams, Predicted Papers and Tutors help students perform under realistic pressure.


The goal is not a flawless rehearsed script. It is the confidence to listen, interpret, respond and continue when the next sentence is not the one you expected.
